IndusEquip Corporation - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusEquip Corporation Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone keypad. There may be a brief pause while we poll for questions. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusEquip Corporation's results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusEquip Corporation's performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, our outlook for end-market growth remains strong in both the near and medium term, supported by robust capex recovery across aerospace, semiconductors, and other key verticals. Second, we've achieved an impressive book-to-bill ratio of 1.15, reflecting accelerating order intake and backlog growth. Third, order intake hit record levels with excellent backlog conversion rates, providing substantial revenue visibility. Fourth, we've made meaningful strides in reducing lead times for our key products and components through supply chain enhancements and capacity expansions. Finally, our cost reduction initiatives are delivering tangible impacts on profitability, with gross margins expanding meaningfully.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Chen to provide more detail on our financial results.

Michael Chen (CFO):
Thank you, John. Turning to our financial performance, IndusEquip Corporation reported $1.83 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 9% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 32.8%, driven by favorable product mix, pricing discipline, and the initial benefits from our cost-saving programs. Operating expenses were $420 million, resulting in an operating income of $210 million. Our net income for the quarter was $150 million, or adjusted EPS of $1.82 per share, up 12% from the prior year.

We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue growth of 8-10% and EPS of $7.50 to $8.00. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

With that foundation, let me expand on the key aspects John highlighted, starting with our outlook for end-market growth in the near and medium term. Our visibility remains strong, underpinned by a $4.2 billion backlog—up 18% from last year—and healthy quoting activity that's 25% ahead of prior-year levels.

In the near term through fiscal 2025, which we view as the next 12-18 months, we anticipate overall end-market growth of 4-6% globally, picking up from the 2-3% seen in fiscal 2024 as supply chains continue to normalize. This growth is propelled by capex recovery in critical sectors, though moderated by softer industrial production in Europe and some selective destocking in discrete automation.

By end market, aerospace and defense, which accounts for 25% of our revenue, should see 8-10% growth, driven by OEM ramp-ups at Boeing and Airbus on narrow-body programs such as the 737 MAX and A320neo. Commercial aftermarket demand is recovering to 85% of pre-pandemic levels, with our precision CNC machining centers and 5-axis mills experiencing 22% quarter-over-quarter order intake gains. Defense spending, supported by U.S. NDAA budgets over $850 billion, bolsters demand for hypersonic and UAV component fabrication, where our book-to-bill reached 1.3 times.

Semiconductor and electronics, 18% of revenue, are poised for 12-15% mid-teens growth as CHIPS Act-funded fabs from TSMC in Arizona and Intel in Ohio ramp up. Global wafer fab equipment spending is forecasted at $110 billion in 2025 according to SEMI, with EUV and high-NA lithography boosting needs for our vacuum systems and robotic wafer handlers. We've noted pull-ins from Samsung and SK Hynix for HBM memory lines linked to AI GPUs.

Automotive and EV, representing 15% of revenue, expect 5-7% growth, as the EV shift offsets slower internal combustion engine volumes. Battery gigafactory expansions—like Tesla's in Nevada and BYD's U.S. entry—are lifting material handling and stamping press orders by 30%. Our electric press brake systems, featuring 20% faster cycle times through servo-hydraulics, are gaining share in lightweighting for 4680 cells.

Renewables and energy, 12% of revenue, should be flat to 3% growth near-term, with wind turbine installations normalizing after IIJA funding peaks. U.S. Northeast offshore wind projects like Vineyard Wind are driving tower welding and nacelle assembly equipment, but Chinese solar module overcapacity is limiting upside.

General industrial and construction, our largest at 30% of revenue, anticipate modest 2-4% growth, aided by 5% gains in non-residential construction from data center builds—hyperscalers like AWS with $75 billion in capex. Our forklifts and AGVs are capitalizing on warehouse automation, even as mining OEMs like Caterpillar and Komatsu pace buys amid commodity swings.

Regionally, North America leads at 6-8% growth, with reshoring adding 1-2 points from IRA incentives—our U.S. utilization is at 92%, and the new Charlotte fab is ramping to 70% capacity. Asia-Pacific follows at 5-7%, powered by India's PLI scheme for semiconductors and China's Made in China 2025 emphasis on high-end machine tools, though export controls on advanced nodes introduce volatility. Europe trails at 1-3%, pressured by energy costs and automotive strikes, offset somewhat by rearmament like Rheinmetall tank production.

Strategically, we're advancing with our EquipEdge IoT platform, now on 40% of new machines, delivering predictive maintenance for 25% uptime improvements and $50 million in recurring SaaS revenue by fiscal 2025 end. We've also expanded hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, partnering with GE Additive on titanium aerospace parts to cut lead times by 40%.

For the medium term through fiscal 2028, we project a robust 8-11% CAGR, surpassing GDP by 500-700 basis points assuming no major recession and 4.5% annual industrial production growth per IHS Markit.

Drivers include Industry 4.0 and automation, with digital twins and cobots expanding—global robot density rising from 140 to 250 units per 10,000 workers per IFR. Our Fanuc-compatible controllers and AI-vision guided welders set us up for over 15% growth in factory automation.

Electrification and decarbonization will see EV penetration at 40% by 2028 per BloombergNEF, spurring $200 billion in battery equipment spend. Hydrogen electrolyzer projects like Plug Power's Tennessee hub and grid-scale storage demand our high-pressure fluid power systems, where electro-hydraulic actuators reduce energy use by 30%.

Reshoring and friendshoring feature U.S. manufacturing PMI above 50 with $1 trillion in announced capex, plus Mexico's nearshoring surge like Tesla's Nuevo Leon site adding 10% regional growth.

Mega-trends such as AI data centers need precision cooling and cleanroom handlers; our cryogenic pumps support Nvidia's Blackwell ramp. Aerospace MRO grows 6% with advanced air mobility certifications like Joby Aviation.

Segment projections show aerospace and defense at 10-12% CAGR, semis and electronics 14-16%, automotive and EV 12-14%, renewables 8-10%, general industrial 6-8%, for total 8-11%.

Risks encompass tariff hikes—10-25% on Chinese imports potentially adding 1-2% cost pressures—labor shortages with 500,000 U.S. skilled trades gaps, and raw material inflation like 15% YTD steel rises. Countermeasures include 60% U.S./Mexico sourcing, $300 million capex for vertical integration in castings, and pricing for 200 basis points EBITDA margin expansion to 22% by fiscal 2027.

Our strategy rests on innovation leadership with 5.5% R&D of sales and 20 new SKUs in fiscal 2025 including 1MW wind blade molds; capacity discipline via 15% throughput adds in Pune and Monterrey brownfields; and customer intimacy with 90% repeat business, co-developing with top OEMs like John Deere for autonomous tractors.

Near-term growth is steady with visibility, medium-term offers megatrend upside. Our fortress balance sheet shows net debt to EBITDA at 1.2 times and ROIC over 20%.

Next, on book-to-bill ratio and trends, which continue to highlight the strength of our $4.2 billion order backlog—adjusted from earlier figures for consistency—in this industrial equipment space. Book-to-bill, new orders over billings, is a vital demand signal given 6-to-18-month cycles for heavy-duty CNC lathes, hydraulic presses, and automated lines.

In Q3, we achieved 1.15 times, up sequentially from 1.08 times in Q2 and 3% year-over-year from 1.12 times in Q3 2023—our best since pre-disruption Q4 2021. This reflects surging orders across industrial automation at 45% of bookings, aerospace and defense at 30%, and energy infrastructure at 25%. Q3 bookings totaled $2.1 billion, up 18% quarter-over-quarter and 12% year-over-year, exceeding $1.83 billion billings up 9% on easier comps.

By segment, industrial automation hit 1.28 times, driven by hyperscaler AI data center capex and factory upgrades—next-gen ServoFlex robotic arms and IoT palletizers up 25% year-over-year with Tesla Gigafactory and Foxconn Vietnam wins. Backlog here is $3.1 billion for 22 months visibility.

Aerospace and defense reached 1.22 times on Boeing and Lockheed ramps post-strikes—$450 million new awards up 30% for 737 MAX fuselages and F-35 spars, with DoD and Airbus tailwinds; backlog $2.8 billion.

Energy infrastructure steady at 1.05 times, LNG offsetting oil softness—$300 million for Chevron Permian hydrogen-ready skids and Shell Prelude upgrades.

Regionally, North America led at 1.25 times from 1.10 times last year via CHIPS Act semis like Intel Ohio and TSMC Arizona for wafer handlers. Europe at 0.98 times amid PMI below 45 and Nord Stream issues, but wind gear from Vestas and Siemens Gamesa emerging. Asia-Pacific at 1.18 times with BYD/CATL EV lines and India's 15% growth in steel roll stands.

Trailing 12-month book-to-bill is 1.12 times from 0.95 times, adding $1.2 billion backlog—top of peers like Caterpillar at 1.05 times, Deere 1.10 times, Honeywell 1.15 times. Utilization at 92% across 15 plants, aided by $450 million fiscal 2024 capex in additive bays and AI supply chains.

Our Resilient Fabrics initiative—$200 million in dual-sourcing rare-earths and titanium—derisks China. EcoForge low-emission presses took 20% bookings at 8-10% premiums amid EU CBAM, shifting mix 5 points to high-margin automation.

We expect Q4 book-to-bill 1.10 to 1.20 times on $4.5 billion bid pipeline, <2% cancellation risk, guiding fiscal 2024 bookings $8.0-8.5 billion.

Turning to order intake expectations and backlog conversion rates, Q3 bookings reached a record $1.28 billion despite segment variances, up 18% year-over-year and 5% sequentially—eighth straight double-digit quarter at 1.25 times book-to-bill above our 1.1 times target.

Automation and robotics led with $520 million up 25%, from FANUC-compatible CNC and ABB cobots in TSMC Arizona and Samsung Texas fabs for sub-5-micron chip packaging.

Heavy machinery $450 million up 12% on LNG in Qatar and U.S. Gulf like Flowserve/Eaton pumps and valves.

Discrete automation $310 million up 15% on Ford/Stellantis EV lines with Siemens-integrated PLCs/SCADA.

Americas 52% at $665 million up 22% from CHIPS/IRA reshoring, Intel Ohio cleanroom handlers. EMEA 28% $360 million up 10% tempered by German autos. APAC 20% $255 million up 8%, offset by China property but boosted by $120 million Reliance green hydrogen.

Full-year 2024 bookings raised to $4.9-5.1 billion, 16-20% growth; Q4 $1.3-1.4 billion on semi/renewables. 2025 visibility 75% of $5.5 billion guide in LOIs/POs. Machinery 4.0 Suite with NVIDIA digital twins at 40% attach lifts ASPs 8-10%; Boeing $280 million 5-year 787 tooling, GE Vernova $150 million H-class.

Q3 backlog $4.7 billion up 22% year-over-year, 7% sequential—record high. Conversion: 42% next 12 months ($2.0 billion), 72% 24 months ($3.4 billion), 92% 36 months. Trailing 12-month 38% in line with norms for long-lead custom vs. short-cycle.

Drivers: 96% on-time delivery from Nucor dual-sourcing and Mexico facility vs. Red Sea issues. Backlog Optimizer ML prioritizes high-margin, 25% gross margin vs. 22% peers like Honeywell/Rockwell. Americas 45%, EMEA 40%, APAC 38% 12-month.

Focused on Industry 4.0 IoT at 30% orders, EV test stands up 35%, low-emission hydraulics for CBAM. China autos 5% backlog risk, steel hedged 80% Q2 2025.

This sets mid-teens growth, 200-300 bps 2025 margins.

On lead times for key products and components, averages improved 22% year-over-year to 16 weeks from 20.5 weeks, down 12% sequentially from Q1's 18.2 weeks via de-risking, expansions, normalization—lower than Caterpillar's 18-20 weeks or Deere's 15-17, aiding $4.7 billion backlog, 1.25 times book-to-bill, 115% FCF.

Key products (65% revenue):

Earthmoving/construction (HX-450 excavators, D-series dozers): 14 weeks, 25% better from Monterrey 250k sq ft facility at 92% utilization, 3-4 week transit cuts. $450 million bookings on IIJA, watch steel tariffs.

Material handling (ApexLift 3000 skid-steers/telehandlers): 12 weeks from 16, 25% gain via modular designs, 30% faster sub-assembly; e-commerce warehouses at 88%.

Mining/aggregates (jaw crushers/conveyors): 20 weeks, 10% better but flat sequential on components; prioritizing copper/lithium miners like Metso/Sandvik clients.

Components (35% aftermarket): supplier leads 10 weeks, 18% down via Supplier Resilience.

Forged steel (chassis/axles): 8 from 12 weeks, 33% via Spartanburg at 95%, dodging China Section 232 duties.

Hydraulics/valves: 9 weeks, 15% better with Bosch Rexroth APAC; AI maintenance cuts defects 40%.

Powertrains: 13 weeks, 12% down despite Tier 4 emissions; 70% dual-sourced U.S./Europe.

Regions: North America 15 weeks best-in-class, onshoring/Houston ports. EMEA 18 weeks on CE/Brexit/Red Sea, Dusseldorf hub +20% intra-EU. APAC 19 weeks post-lockdowns, buffers for Indonesia/Australia mining like Rio Tinto $6B.

Pillars: $150M digital (SAP S/4HANA, 95% forecast accuracy, 35% less stockouts); diversification (45% Asia from 60%, China+1 Vietnam/India); capacity (20% machining via Fanuc robotics, JIT/25% buffer).

Q4 guide 15-17 weeks, supports 8-10% FY24 revenue, 150bps EBITDA to 22%; NPS 72, share in $1.2T market.

Finally, our cost reduction initiatives and profitability impact amid 12% steel inflation, Red Sea delays, construction softness: $185 million YTD run-rate savings, 240bps gross to 32.8%, 450bps EBITDA to 18.2%.

Supply chain/procurement 55% ($100M ann.): suppliers 450 to 320, 8-10% discounts; Nucor steel -15% costs vs. Section 301 tariffs. Monterrey nearshoring 25% hydraulics, -40% freight/lead to 6 weeks; Eastern Europe 30% vs. Asia CBAM 5-7%; Asia hedging 70% Q3 at $650/ton.

Operational 30% ($55M): $120M Industry 4.0 capex, MindSphere at Rockford VeriCut CNC -28% downtime, OEE 82-91% like DMG Mori; ABB robotic welds -22% cycles on excavators, 12k hours saved; VFD spindles -18% energy.

SG&A 15% ($30M): distributors 1200 to 950, turns 5.2-6.8x; 4% headcount attrition to automation roles; Warsaw hub -22% EMEA admin.

Q3 COGS -7% sales %, op income +32% $210M, FCF $150M +50%, $75M buybacks/debt paydown. H2 +$50M, gross 34% vs. 29% industry. Resilience for IRA/ev-hyrdraulics 25%+ margins.

Q4 embeds $45M more, aluminum/election risks.

Now, I will hand over to Lisa Patel, COO, for an operational update.

Lisa Patel (COO):
Thank you, Michael. Operationally, we've been focused on streamlining our supply chain and improving manufacturing efficiency. We have implemented several new initiatives that are already yielding positive results, including further optimizations in our digital transformation efforts and capacity utilization across plants. We are closely monitoring the global supply chain situation and taking proactive steps to mitigate any potential disruptions, such as ongoing diversification and inventory buffering. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies like advanced IoT and AI to enhance our operational capabilities, which ties directly into our lead time reductions and backlog execution.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, press star one one. Our first question comes from Ben Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Ben Smith (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

Michael Chen:
Thanks, Ben. Rising raw materials like steel up 12% year-over-year have been a headwind, but our cost initiatives have more than offset it. Through supplier consolidation to 320 partners with locked discounts, domestic Nucor sourcing cutting costs 15%, nearshoring hydraulics production, and hedging 70-80% exposures, we've captured $185 million run-rate savings YTD. This drove 240 basis points gross margin expansion to 32.8% and supports our 34% year-end target. We're positioned resiliently with pricing discipline adding another layer of protection.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen (Goldman Sachs):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

John Reynolds:
Good question, Emily. Aftermarket remains a bright spot, rebounding strongly in aerospace to 85% pre-pandemic with MRO growth at 6% medium-term on AAM like Joby. In semis and autos, our IoT-enabled predictive maintenance via EquipEdge on 40% new machines is driving $50 million SaaS recurring by 2025, with 25% uptime gains boosting attach rates. We see mid-teens growth here, margin-accretive at 35-40%, as reshoring and electrification extend equipment lifecycles.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

Lisa Patel:
Absolutely, David. We've compressed average lead times 22% year-over-year to 16 weeks, with sequential 12% improvement. For earthmoving gear like our excavators, down 25% to 14 weeks via Monterrey ramp; material handling to 12 weeks on modular designs; mining steady at 20 but prioritized. Components like forgings to 8 weeks through Spartanburg vertical integration, hydraulics to 9 weeks with Bosch partnerships. Regional wins in North America at 15 weeks from onshoring. Our digital SAP rollout, supplier diversification to 45% Asia, and 20% capacity adds position us for 15-17 weeks in Q4, enhancing competitiveness.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time.

John Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions and your interest in IndusEquip Corporation. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
